title: Learning from Delayed Rewards
headline: An agent can learn the best thing to do in every situation with no map of its world, just by edging a table of move-by-move scores toward each reward it bumps into, until the value of a distant goal seeps backward through every step that leads to it.
abstract: In behavioural ecology, stochastic dynamic programming may be used as a general method for calculating animals' optimal behavioural policies. But how might the animals themselves learn optimal policies from their experience? The aim of the thesis is to give a systematic analysis of possible computational methods of learning efficient behaviour. First, it is argued that it does follow from the optimality assumption that animals should learn optimal policies, even though they may not always follow them. Next, it is argued that Markov decision processes are a general formal model of an animal's behavioural choices in its environment. The conventional methods of determining optimal policies by dynamic programming are then described. It is not plausible that animals carry out calculations of this type. However, there is a range of alternative methods of organising the dynamic programming calculation, in ways that are plausible computational models of animal learning. In particular, there is an incremental Monte-Carlo method that enables the optimal values (or 'canonical costs') of actions to be learned directly, without any requirement for the animal to model its environment, or to remember situations and actions for more than a short period of time. A proof is given that this learning method works. Learning methods of this type are also possible for hierarchical policies. Previously suggested learning methods are reviewed, and some even simpler learning methods are presented without proof. Demonstration implementations of some of the learning methods are described.

images.alt: A top-down pixel dungeon grid on aged parchment with a glowing clay-orange treasure chest labelled Goal in the corner, its warm glow fading room by room across the grid while a short ink arrow in every room points toward the chest, showing that a reward at the goal seeps backward until every spot knows the way to it.
images.caption: The reward at the goal backs up cell by cell until every cell's arrow points the way to it.

images.alt: Two pixel stone rooms labelled now and next on parchment, a clay-orange reward coin between them, an ink arrow leaving the now room through a door and a curved ink arrow feeding the glowing next room's value back to revise the number written on the door, showing that one step nudges a single move's score toward the reward plus the best value of where it leads.
images.caption: Each step nudges one move's score toward the reward you just got plus the best you can do from where you land.

images.alt: A pixel dungeon on parchment with a treasure chest in the corner, a meandering sage-green dashed path labelled wander tracing an explorer's random route, and a separate field of clean solid black ink arrows in every room all pointing along the shortest route to the chest labelled learn, showing that an agent can wander any way it likes and still learn the one best route.
images.caption: Wander any way you like, even at random, and the learned best route still points straight at the goal.

images.alt: A row of pixel stone rooms on parchment leading away from a glowing clay-orange treasure chest labelled goal, the warm glow a clear notch dimmer in each room further off, with an ink bracket under each room and a distance arrow beneath, showing that a far-off reward is worth a little less with every step so its value fades with distance.
images.caption: The discount makes far-off treasure worth a little less each step, so its value fades with distance.
